deities: Lord Rama, Sita and Lakshmana (idols at the summit)

history.period: Ancient (legendary); summit Yama temple built/restored by Rani Ahilyabai Holkar, 18th century
history.summary: Pretshila ('Ghost Hill' - preta + shila) is the highest of the seven hills around Gaya, about 8 km north-west of the city, and one of the 48 surviving vedis (of the 360 named in the Vayu Purana) for Pind Daan. It is prescribed especially for ancestors who died unnatural deaths (accident, suicide), whose souls are believed to linger in preta form until rites here release them. The climb is nearly 600 steps from Brahma Kunda at the foot; the summit has the sacred rock itself (said to be the thumb of Tirtha Vichitra Shila of Narayana, sprung from Prabhasa Mountain), a temple of Lord Yama attributed to Rani Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore (renovated several times), shrines of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, idols of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, the footprint of Brahma with three golden lines, and the Ramkund tank where Rama is said to have bathed. Legends hold that Rama and Lakshmana performed Dasharatha's Pind Daan here, and that Yamaraja built Preta Parvat on the Dharma Shila. Two rooms at the summit serve shraddha rituals; palanquin/doli bearers are available for those who cannot climb.

name: Pretshila Hill Temples
town_description: Gaya, in southern Bihar on the Falgu river about 100 km south of Patna, is one of Hinduism's holiest cities - the principal centre for ancestor rites (Pind Daan and Shraddha), anchored by the Vishnupad Temple. It is a district headquarters with a 2011 population of about 470,000 and sits about 13 km from Bodh Gaya, the Buddhist pilgrimage centre. Pretshila Hill lies about 8 km north-west of the city centre.
tradition: Hinduism (pitr/shraddha tradition; Shaivite and Vaishnavite shrines at the summit)

travel.airport: Gaya Airport, approx. 12-13 km; taxis and app cabs available.
travel.railway: Gaya Junction approx. 8-9 km; autos and taxis to the hill base.
travel.road: Approx. 8 km north-west of Gaya city centre; local transport to the base, then nearly 600 steps to the summit. Palanquin/doli bearers are available for those unable to climb.

visitor_information.best_time: September to October (Pitru Paksha) is the principal ritual season, when thousands of pilgrims gather; October to March for weather. Early morning is best for the climb.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Daylight hours typical; an open ritual site generally accessible morning to evening (verify - not documented in the sources consulted). Photography inside the temple premises may be restricted - check signage.
